title: Englisch 9: Participle Clauses, Gerund vs. Infinitiv und The British Empire & Commonwealth (Gymnasium 9 Bayern)
description: Geerdetes KVT-Paket für Gymnasium Bayern Englisch 9 (E1/E2): Partizipialkonstruktionen zur Satzverkürzung (Present/Past Participle clauses replacing relative & adverbial clauses), Gerund vs. Infinitiv (Verben mit Bedeutungsunterschied: remember, stop, forget, try), Modal auxiliaries in the past (could have, should have, must have done) sowie Cultural Studies zu British Empire, Dekolonisation, Commonwealth of Nations und multikultureller Identität in Großbritannien und Australien.

sources.label: Gymnasium Englisch 9, Lernbereiche Sprachliche Mittel – Syntax und Partizipien, Interkulturelle Kompetenzen

atoms.title: Englische Grammatik 9: Participle Clauses, Gerund vs. Infinitive und Modale Hilfsverben der Vergangenheit

practice_items.question: Welche Bedeutung hat der Satz mit Gerundium: 'He stopped smoking.' im Vergleich zu 'He stopped to smoke.'?
practice_items.concept: Er gab das Rauchen dauerhaft auf (Gegenteil: 'He stopped to smoke' = Er hielt an, um eine Zigarette zu rauchen)

options: Er hörte mit dem Rauchen auf (Aufgabe einer Gewohnheit)
Er hielt an, um eine Zigarette zu rauchen

practice_items.question: Analysiere Participle Clauses, Gerund vs. Infinitive und Modal Auxiliaries in the Past: 1. **Participle Clauses (Partizipialsätze zur Satzverkürzung)**:   * **Present Participle (-ing)**: Ersetzt Aktivsätze bei Gleichzeitigkeit oder Kausalität (*'Seeing the police, the thief ran away'* = When/Because he saw the police...).   * **Past Participle (3rd form / -ed)**: Ersetzt Passivsätze (*'Built in 1889, the Eiffel Tower is famous'* = As it was built in 1889...).   * **Having + Past Participle**: Drückt Vorzeitigkeit im Aktiv aus (*'Having finished her homework, she met her friends'* = After she had finished...), 2. **Gerund vs. Infinitive bei Bedeutungsunterschied**:   * *stop + Gerund* (Aufhören mit Tätigkeit) vs. *stop + to-Infinitive* (Unterbrechung, um etwas anderes zu tun).   * *remember / forget + Gerund* (Rückblickende Erinnerung an eine vergangene Handlung) vs. *+ to-Infinitive* (Vorausschauend an eine Pflicht denken), 3. **Modal Auxiliaries in the Past**: *must have done* (logische Schlussfolgerung), *should have done* (versäumte Pflicht/Vorwurf), *could have done* (nicht genutzte Möglichkeit), *can't/couldn't have done* (Unmöglichkeit).
practice_items.concept: Participle Clauses: Present Participle (Aktiv/gleichzeitig), Past Participle (Passiv), Having + 3rd form (Vorzeitigkeit); Gerund vs. Infinitiv mit Bedeutungswechsel (stop, remember, forget); Modale Hilfsverben in der Vergangenheit (must/should/could have + 3rd form).
practice_items.sample_solution: 1. Participle Clauses (Kompakte Syntax zur Satzstraffung): - Partizipialsätze ersetzen Relativ-, Zeit- oder Kausalsätze, wenn Haupt- und Nebensatz dasselbe Subjekt teilen:   * **1. Present Participle (-ing) [Aktiv & Gleichzeitigkeit / Kausalität]**:     - *« **Walking** through the park, I met an old friend. »* (While I was walking...).     - *« **Feeling** tired, she went to bed early. »* (Because she felt tired...).   * **2. Past Participle (-ed / 3. Form) [Passiv]**:     - *« **Surrounded** by high mountains, the village is very quiet. »* (As it is surrounded...).   * **3. Perfect Participle (Having + Past Participle) [Aktiv & Vorzeitigkeit]**:     - *« **Having passed** his driving test, Tom bought a car. »* (After he had passed his test...). 2. Gerund vs. Infinitiv mit gravierendem Bedeutungsunterschied: | Verb | Mit Gerund (-ing) [Handlung fand statt] | Mit to-Infinitiv [Handlung soll stattfinden] | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **stop** | *« He stopped smoking. »* (Er gab das Rauchen auf) | *« He stopped to smoke. »* (Er hielt an, um zu rauchen) | | **remember** | *« I remember locking the door. »* (Ich erinnere mich daran, zugeschlossen zu haben) | *« Remember to lock the door! »* (Denk daran, abzuschließen!) | | **forget** | *« I'll never forget meeting the Queen. »* (Ich vergesse nie die Begegnung) | *« Don't forget to call Mum! »* (Vergiss nicht anzurufen!) | | **try** | *« Try taking an aspirin. »* (Probier es als Experiment aus) | *« Try to open the window. »* (Streng dich an, es zu öffnen) | 3. Modal Auxiliaries in the Past (Vermutungen und verpasste Gelegenheiten): - **must have + 3. Form**: Nahezu sichere logische Schlussfolgerung in der Vergangenheit (*« The streets are wet; it **must have rained** last night. »*). - **should / ought to have + 3. Form**: Eine Pflicht oder ein Rat, der in der Vergangenheit versäumt wurde (*« You **should have studied** harder for the exam. »*). - **could have + 3. Form**: Fähigkeit/Möglichkeit, die nicht realisiert wurde (*« You **could have helped** me, but you just watched. »*). - **can't / couldn't have + 3. Form**: Absolute Unmöglichkeit (*« He **can't have stolen** the money; he was in Paris. »*).

atoms.title: Cultural Studies: The British Empire, Decolonisation, the Commonwealth of Nations and Australia

prerequisites.rationale: Landeskundliche Textanalyse und Mediation erfordern fortgeschrittene Syntax.

curricula.topic_title: Landeskunde – The British Empire and Commonwealth

practice_items.question: What is the primary modern purpose of the Commonwealth of Nations, comprising 56 independent member states?
practice_items.concept: A voluntary association of independent sovereign nations fostering democracy, human rights, trade, and cultural exchange

options: Voluntary association of independent states promoting cooperation
A military alliance under British command

practice_items.question: Analyse the historical development from the British Empire to the modern Commonwealth and multicultural Britain: 1. **The British Empire (Peak in the late 19th/early 20th century)**:   * *'The empire on which the sun never sets'*: Covered a quarter of the world's landmass and population.   * Motivations: Economic exploitation (raw materials like tea, spices, cotton, minerals), trade routes, and ideological 'civilizing mission' (Rudyard Kipling's *'White Man's Burden'*).   * India as the *'Jewel in the Crown'*, 2. **Decolonisation & Independence**: Post-WWII decline, Indian Independence in 1947 led by Mahatma Gandhi (non-violent resistance / Satyagraha), 'Wind of Change' across Africa in the 1950s/1960s, 3. **The Commonwealth of Nations**: 56 voluntary sovereign countries; regular Commonwealth Games and summits promoting democracy, education, and development, 4. **Multicultural Britain & Migration**: The arrival of the *Empire Windrush* (1948) from the Caribbean; post-war immigration from South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh); cultural diversity, culinary fusion, challenges of integration, and contemporary debates on postcolonial identity.
practice_items.concept: British Empire: Expansion, economic exploitation & 'civilizing mission'; Decolonisation (Gandhi 1947, African independence); Modern Commonwealth (56 sovereign states); Multicultural Britain (Windrush generation 1948, South Asian migration, diversity).
practice_items.sample_solution: 1. The Rise and Reach of the British Empire: - **Geographic Scale**: By the early 20th century, the British Empire was the largest empire in human history, governing over **400 million people (approx. 25% of the globe's population)** across five continents (*« The empire on which the sun never sets »*). - **Motivations and Methods**:   * **Economic Extraction**: Triangular slave trade, control of global maritime trade routes (East India Company), extraction of precious commodities (rubber from Malaya, tea and cotton from India, gold from South Africa).   * **Imperialist Ideology**: Justified through eurocentric notions of racial superiority and a paternalistic *« civilizing mission »*. - **India**: Termed the *« Jewel in the Crown »*, administered by the British Raj from 1858 until 1947. 2. Decolonisation and the End of Empire: - **Factors**: Britain's economic exhaustion following World War II, combined with rising nationalist independence movements across Asia and Africa. - **Key Milestones**:   * **1947**: Independence and tragic Partition of India and Pakistan, achieved under the moral leadership of **Mahatma Gandhi's** philosophy of *Ahimsa* (non-violence) and civil disobedience.   * **1950s–1960s**: The *« Wind of Change »* (Harold Macmillan, 1960) led to rapid independence for African nations (e.g., Ghana 1957, Nigeria 1960, Kenya 1963). 3. The Modern Commonwealth of Nations: - **Structure**: A voluntary association of **56 independent and equal sovereign states** (most former British territories, but also nations like Rwanda and Mozambique). - **Values**: Anchored in the Commonwealth Charter: commitment to international peace, democratic governance, rule of law, gender equality, and sustainable development. 4. Post-War Migration and Multicultural Britain: - **The Windrush Generation (1948)**:   * Arrival of the *HMT Empire Windrush* carrying citizens from Jamaica and the Caribbean invited to help rebuild war-torn Britain (working in the NHS, London Underground, and manufacturing). - **South Asian Immigration**: Large communities from India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh settled in industrial urban hubs (London, Birmingham, Manchester, Bradford). - **Impact**: Transformation of Britain into a vibrant, diverse multicultural society, reflected in arts, politics, literature, and everyday cuisine (e.g., Chicken Tikka Masala becoming a national dish), alongside ongoing discussions surrounding institutional racism and historical reparations.
